modern: Theophrastus, in his comparison of bad acts—such a comparison as one would make in keeping with the common notions of mankind—says, like a true philosopher, that the offences committed through desire are more blameworthy than those committed through anger. For he who is stirred by anger seems to turn away from reason with a certain pain and unconscious contraction; but he who offends through desire, being overpowered by pleasure, seems in a way to be more intemperate and more womanish in his offences. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the offence committed with pleasure is more blameworthy than that committed with pain; and on the whole the one is more like a person who has first been wronged and through pain is driven to anger, while the other is moved by his own impulse to do wrong, being carried towards doing something by desire.
original: Theophrastus, in his comparison of bad acts—such a comparison as one would make in accordance with the common notions of mankind—says, like a true philosopher, that the offenses which are committed through desire are more blamable than those which are committed through anger. For he who is excited by anger seems to turn away from reason with a certain pain and unconscious contraction; but he who offends through desire, being overpowered by pleasure, seems to be in a manner more intemperate and more womanish in his offences. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the offence which is committed with pleasure is more blamable than that which is committed with pain; and on the whole the one is more like a person who has been first wronged and through pain is compelled to be angry, but the other is moved by his own impulse to do wrong, being carried towards doing something by desire.

explained.summary:
Theophrastus, the Greek philosopher who studied under Aristotle, argued that wrongs done out of desire are worse than wrongs done out of anger, and Marcus agrees. An angry person turns away from reason in pain, often in reaction to being hurt. Someone who does wrong for pleasure chooses it freely and enjoys it.

It’s a striking reversal of what we might expect: the cool, comfortable self-indulgence can be worse than the hot outburst.
explained.today: Snapping at a partner after a terrible day is wrong, but it’s different from deliberately lying to them to enjoy something on the side. The first comes from pain; the second is a choice made for pleasure.
